paragraphs.text: Once upon a time, there was a young prince. He smiled and laughed all day long.
His parents, the king and queen, always said, "You're the perfect child!" And they made sure the prince got everything he ever wanted.
And reader, I mean everything !
He said, "I want a pony!" His parents gave him ten. He said, "I want a new belt!" They gave him one with two rubies and a sapphire.
You might think that was why the prince was so happy. But you'd be wrong.
The prince was happy because he never got into trouble. Not even when he behaved badly, which was most days!
A nursemaid, Nana, watched over the prince. Nana was loving and gentle—and very good at her job.
Every day she'd gently remind him, "You are a very smart boy."
Every night she'd tuck him into bed. "A wonderful future awaits you, my precious prince."
But there was one thing Nana hadn't yet succeeded in doing. And it bothered her deeply.
"I was sent to this castle for one reason. I must make sure he becomes a kind king."
So, she kept trying to teach him to be kind.
"Your kingdom has many poor and sad families," she'd say.
The prince would just shrug. "Oh well! My family is rich and happy!"
Nana finally went to the king for advice. When the king heard how his son was acting, he grinned. "Wonderful news! He will make a fine king one day!"
Next, Nana went to the queen. But the queen covered her ears. "My son is a perfect angel!"
Nana knew then that she was all on her own. She was the only one who could teach the prince about kindness. But time was running out.
"The prince is growing up," she thought. "Soon he won't need me anymore. Yet his heart is growing harder and colder by the day."
It was time to do something—something magical.
You see, reader, Nana wasn't just a nursemaid. She was a fairy. And it was the fairy queen who had sent her there.
"The next king must be kind and fair," the fairy queen had said.
Nana had never used magic at the castle before.
"But now," she thought, "I will do what I must do."
A few days later, the king and queen left the castle. They were going to visit a king in a faraway land. Nana and the prince waved good-bye from the castle steps.
"Nana, take care of my precious boy," the queen said.
"Bring me presents!" the prince shouted as the carriage rolled away.
Nana sighed. This was her chance to try a magic spell. But magic was serious. Fairies used it only when they had to. She decided to talk to the prince one last time.
"Prince, one day you'll rule this kingdom. You must have a kind and generous heart. Please show me that you can be kind."
"Okay." The prince looked around. "I see some servant girls. I'll ask if they need anything."
He ran to the servants. "You're working so hard. Can I bring you a refreshment?"
The servant girls looked surprised.
"Why, um, certainly, Your Highness," one said.
"Great! I'll get some fruit." The prince dashed into the castle. He returned with a bowl of fruit.
Nana beamed. "He's learning!" she thought. "Maybe magic isn't needed after all!"
But then the prince laughed and threw the fruit at them.
"Stop that!" Nana pulled the prince away. "I've tried to teach you to be kind. But your heart is as cold as stone. So, I must do what I must do."
The prince laughed. "Like what?"
"Like this!"
Poof! The prince turned into a statue of stone covered in gold.
"You will stand frozen above the village, watching your people. Seeing their struggles will surely soften your heart."
"Break this spell now!" the statue cried.
"Only you can do that," Nana said. "Tell me when you know how to be kind."
Days passed. Nana waited, nervously watching the statue.
"Surely the prince sees the people's troubles now," she thought. "And surely he wants to help them."
But the statue stayed silent.
Then one day news came. The king and queen were returning home. Nana ran to the statue.
"I can't let them see my magic spell," she thought.
She tried to break the spell herself. But nothing worked—the magic was too strong.
Nana buried her face in her hands. "The king will throw me into the dungeon! I must leave at once!"
Poof! Nana disappeared, leaving the statue all alone.
The king and queen stared at the stone statue in horror.
"That's not our son!" the king said.
"My baby has been kidnapped!" the queen cried. "And the villains left a statue in his place."
"This is Nana's fault!" the king growled. "Guards! Find her, then throw her in the dungeon!"
But, reader, the guards could not find Nana. And the prince's parents couldn't bear to look at the statue. So, they sent it to a town far from the castle.
The townspeople were happy to have such a beautiful statue. It was made of stone but covered in gleaming gold. Three sparkling jewels sat in its belt.
Often the people gathered at the statue's base, talking about it.
"We're so lucky to have this statue!"
"Look at his smile!"
"Let's call him the Happy Prince!"
One day a flock of swallows flew over the town.
"This looks like a nice place," their leader said. "We'll spend the rest of the summer here. Then we'll fly to Egypt for the winter."
And that's exactly what the swallows did. Most of them stayed in town. But one swallow liked to spend his time at the lake.
One day the leader flew to talk to him.
"Please join the rest of the flock," Leader said. "Summer is almost over. We will leave for Egypt soon."
"I'm not going to Egypt," Swallow said. "Because I am in love!"
"Ugh, not again," Leader thought. But he smiled politely.
"With who?" he asked.
"Come! I'll introduce you to my love!" Swallow said.
He led Leader out over the water. As they flew, Swallow said, "She is the most beautiful thing in the world!"
Now, every bird knew that Swallow loved beautiful things. He fell in love every season.
"Hmm," Leader thought. "Is he talking about the lake this time? The sunset? Another bird maybe?"
That's when Swallow landed lightly on a tall reed.
Leader gasped. "Your love is a reed?"
"Yes." Swallow smiled. "Isn't she beautiful?"
Leader didn't want to be rude. And, reader, neither do I! Don't get me wrong—she was a lovely reed. She swayed in the breeze. She held Swallow gently when he landed on her.
But she was still a reed!
Leader blinked a few times. "I hope you change your mind. Winter is coming. It will get very cold here."
Swallow didn't reply. He just smiled and stared at his beloved reed.

Back in town the statue was also staring at something. He had no choice but to stare at the town all day. His body was frozen in place. But he was alive inside his golden shell, watching people pass by.
"Nana will pay for what's she done to me," he thought angrily. "If I ever escape this statue, that is!"
One morning a group of townspeople began gathering at his base.
"Here they are again!" the statue thought in frustration. "Every day they come and stand by me. And all they do is talk, talk, talk! Grr! I wish I had some fruit to throw at them!"
Usually, the townspeople talked about how proud they were of the statue.
"His gold shines!"
"His jewels sparkle!"
"Look at his smile. Seeing him makes me happy too!"
But this day was different. People weren't talking about the statue's smile. They weren't admiring his gold or jewels. They were complaining—a lot!
"I lost my farm," one man said. "I couldn't pay my taxes to the king."
"I had to sell my shoes to buy food," a woman said.
Others began calling out their problems. And reader, they had a lot of serious problems.
"Grr," the statue thought. "If I could move my hands, I'd put them over my ears!"
But he couldn't move. So, he had no choice but to listen.
Soon the mayor arrived and quieted the crowd. "Why are you complaining? It was good of the king to give us this beautiful statue."
"Exactly!" the statue thought. "I make this ugly town much prettier!"
But then a girl, not much older than the prince, spoke up. "We like the statue. But it's not a person. Why does it need all that gold?"
"Its beauty doesn't help the poor," a woman added.
"We could buy a lot of food with those jewels!" somebody shouted.
The girl nodded. "What good is beauty if we're poor and hungry?"
The statue wanted to stay angry. But he was beginning to feel something strange and new.
"My chest feels funny," he thought.
Then he remembered something Nana had said. "Your heart is as cold and heavy as stone."
"It's my heart," the statue realized. "Nana was right. I have a cold and heavy heart."
Summer was coming to an end. Townspeople continued to gather at the statue. Some came to admire it. Others enjoyed its smile. But most still came to talk about their problems.
The statue listened to everything they said. Hearing people's problems every day was hard. And it was making him sad. Even compliments about his beauty couldn't make him happy anymore.
"I never knew life was so hard," he thought. "But now I do. If only I could stop smiling, I could show people that I'm listening to their pain. But like my heart, my smile is made of heavy stone."
A few days later, Swallow flew over the town. He was looking for a gift to bring to his love.
"I want something as beautiful as she is," he thought.
He spotted some daisies down on a hilltop. But they had begun to wilt. So Swallow flew on until he saw an apple orchard.
"I'll bring her a bright red apple," he thought.
But none of the apples looked right. At last, Swallow spotted the perfect thing. A rosebush was growing under a statue.
"Hooray!" Swallow cheered. "I'll pick the most perfect rose!"

Swallow swooped toward the rosebush. But as he flew past the statue, something flashed in his eye. It was the statue's gold, gleaming brightly in the sun. Its three jewels sparkled like stars at night.
Swallow gasped at its beauty. "This statue would be the finest gift for my love. If only it wasn't so big and heavy! Oh well. A perfect rose will do."
Swallow continued toward the roses when he heard a moan. He looked around but didn't see anyone.
"Who's there?"
No one answered. There was another moan. It sounded like it was coming from the statue.
"It couldn't be the statue," Swallow thought. "It looks so happy. And nothing that beautiful could ever be sad. Besides, statues don't talk. Do they? It must have been the wind."
Swallow started looking for the best rose when his flock landed nearby.
"Swallow! Come along," Leader called. "It's time to fly to Egypt."
"Have a good trip," Swallow said. "I'm staying here, near my love."
Leader frowned. "Winter is coming. You'll freeze."
"I have my love to keep me warm," Swallow said.
"You're making a mistake," Leader said. "But if you insist, then I wish you good luck."
"I won't need it!" Swallow said as the flock flew away.
As Swallow watched the flock go, he felt a little sad. He'd been born into that flock. The other birds were his family. He'd miss them. Still, he knew in his heart he'd made the right choice.
"I never want to leave my love again," he thought. "This perfect rose will show her I care."
Swallow flew back to the lake. He swooped and dove over the water. He flew in fancy circles and loops.
"I hope my reed is watching," he thought. "She'll see what a great and fast flyer I am! And she'll love this rose."
Swallow came in for a landing as the sun was setting. But something was wrong. His beautiful reed had disappeared! In her place was a bent and wilted brown reed.
"My most beautiful reed wilted!" Swallow thought. "This is the worst thing that has ever happened to me!"
Swallow felt crushed. But then his situation got worse. A cold wind began to blow.
Swallow shivered. "Brr! Leader was right. I'll freeze here. I need to find my flock right away."
Swallow dropped the rose where his love stood wilting and took off. He flew as fast as he could. But the wind was sharp and strong. And he didn't see the flock anywhere.
"I'll find them in the morning," he thought. "For now, I just need a warm place to sleep."
Swallow looked around the town. "There's that beautiful statue. It's the perfect place to spend the night."
Swallow landed between the statue's two feet. "It's nice and warm here," he thought.
Swallow tucked his head under his wing. Nearby two women were talking loudly.
"My gown for the king's ball is going to be beautiful!" one said. "But that lazy seamstress still hasn't finished it!"
"Why not?" asked the other.
"Something about her son. I think he has a cold."
Swallow, who loved beautiful things, wished he could see this lovely gown.
"But I must leave early in the morning," he thought.
He closed his eyes. Plop! A drop of rain fell on his head, then another, and another.
"Oh bother!" he grumbled. "This isn't a good place to sleep after all."
Swallow flew upward. He expected to get soaking wet. But there were no clouds. And there was no rain.
Swallow blinked in surprise. The water was coming from the statue!
Swallow flew around the statue. "Where is the water coming from?" he thought.
Then he saw the statue's eyes. He gasped. "Are those tears streaming from his eyes? It can't be."
But it was!
Swallow perched on the statue's shoulder for a closer look. And indeed, tears were flowing from the statue's eyes.
"But statues don't cry," Swallow said. "Especially not happy statues."
"Well, looks aren't everything!" a voice said.
"Who said that?" Swallow looked around. There was no one there.
Swallow shook his head. "I've got to get out of this town. Strange things are happening! Statues that cry. A voice from nowhere. I will leave for Egypt at first light!"
"At least you can leave," the voice said.
Swallow couldn't believe it. The statue was talking to him!
He flapped his wings. "Are you alive in there?"
"Yes, I am." The statue sighed deeply.
"How did you get inside a statue?" Swallow asked.

"It was a magic spell. I used to be a boy, and I was so happy. I didn't have a care in the world," the statue said. "My parents, the king and queen, loved me very much. They said I was perfect. Everyone at the castle called me the Happy Prince."
"You still look happy. So why are you crying?" Swallow asked.
"Because now I'm sad all the time," the statue said.
"I guess I'd be sad too, if I was a statue. Then I couldn't fly fast like this!" Swallow zoomed around the statue. "Or look at beautiful things—like you and my darling. Well, never mind."
"I wish I was a boy again," the statue said. "But that's not why I'm crying. It's because so many people are sad."
"They are?" Swallow said. "I never noticed."
"My nursemaid tried to teach me to think about others. But I never listened," the statue said. "And now all I see is the misery of the world. Yet I am helpless to do anything about it."
"Your smile must make people happy," Swallow said.
The statue scoffed. "My smile doesn't feed them. It doesn't keep them warm at night."
After that, the statue stopped talking. Swallow rested near the statue’s feet. Swallow thought about telling the prince about his reed. She was now brown and wilted. But he stopped himself.
"This statue doesn't need to hear another sad story!" Swallow thought.
The next morning Swallow was eager to catch up to the flock. He flew up to say good-bye to the statue.
"Thank you for keeping me warm last night," he said.
The statue sighed. "You're welcome. Thank you for listening to my sad story."
"I hope you find a way to be happy," Swallow said.
"I won't—not until everyone has what he or she needs."
Swallow never had to think about what anyone else needed. The flock leader did that. Leader looked after all the birds.
"Too bad there's nothing you can do," Swallow said.
"There are things that I could do," the statue said. "If only I could move."
Perhaps the swallow should have left then. But he had been thinking about the statue's unhappiness. He had been thinking about the townspeople's misery too.
"Tell me your idea, Prince."
Swallow listened carefully. "You're sure you want to do this?"
"Absolutely!"
"Okay," Swallow said. "First, I'll do what you asked. Then I'll leave for Egypt. I hope this will make you happier."
"Thank you, Swallow."
Swallow flew down to the statue's belt. He gripped one of the rubies with his beak and pulled. Then he flew off, carrying the jewel.
Swallow flew to the edge of town. He soon spotted where the statue had told him to go. It was a one-room house.
He looked inside. The room was empty except for a table and bed. A woman sat at the table sewing a dress. But this wasn't just any dress. It was a beautiful ballgown covered in shiny crystals.
Swallow gasped. "That's stunning! She doesn't need this jewel. I'll return it to the statue and then leave for Egypt!"
Swallow hopped to the edge of the windowsill. He was about to take flight when someone began coughing.
Swallow looked closer. It was a little boy. He looked very sick.
"My poor baby," the woman said. "We will have money for medicine soon. As soon as I finish this ballgown for a lady."
"Oh!" Swallow realized. "The seamstress is making the dress for someone else. She really does need this jewel."
Whoosh! Swallow zoomed inside and dropped the jewel in the woman's lap. Then he flew out the window before she could see him.
The woman gasped. "A gift from above! It seems impossible. But now I can buy my boy his medicine!"
After dropping the jewel, Swallow felt wonderful.
"I'm so glad I stayed to help the prince," he thought. "And the seamstress. Now it's time to leave for Egypt."
Swallow began flying east. But he wasn't alone. A large hawk was flying right above him.
"Oh no!" Swallow thought. "That hawk looks hungry!"
Swoosh! Swallow switched directions and flew back to town. The hawk did not follow him.
"Phew! That was scary," Swallow thought.
He was about to begin the journey again. Suddenly he heard a long, deep moan.
"That's Prince! Is he in trouble?"
Swallow zoomed back. The statue was crying again.
"Prince! Why are you sad?" Swallow asked. "The seamstress was so grateful for the jewel. Now she can buy her son's medicine."
"Thank you." The statue sniffed. "But there are so many more people like her. Poor, sick, and unhappy."
Swallow sighed. "What if I help someone else? Would that make you feel better?"
"What about Egypt?"
"I will go tomorrow," Swallow said. "I can't leave while you're so sad."
The next day Swallow plucked the other ruby from the statue's belt. Then he flew to the docks by the river.
At one dock a captain was talking to his crew. "Finish loading the ship. We set sail for Egypt today!"
"That's where I'm going!" Swallow thought. "See you there! But first, my errand for the prince."
Swallow swooped through crowds, past mothers with crying children. He picked up breadcrumbs and dropped them for hungry dogs.
"Everyone needs something," he thought. "But I can't help everyone . I need to find the person I'm looking for. Then I'll leave for Egypt, just like that ship."
At last, Swallow spotted her. He dove through the crowd and landed near a young girl. She wore a thin sweater and was shivering. In her hands she held a basket of eggs.
"Eggs for sale! Please, buy my eggs," she called.
A woman stopped and curled her lip. "No one will buy broken eggs!"
"But I must sell some! Or I'll have no money to bring to the orphanage," the girl said. "Then we'll all go hungry!"
The woman shrugged and walked away.
Swallow felt a pang in his chest.
"How unkind," he thought.
He flew closer to the girl. Then he carefully dropped the jewel into her basket.
Once more, Swallow felt proud after his good deed. And once more, he was ready to go.
He searched the docks for the ship to Egypt. He didn't need to follow it—he knew the way. But traveling alone seemed lonely and tiring.
Swallow spotted the ship and started to dive down. But a hawk was circling overhead. It was the same one that Swallow had seen yesterday.
"If I land, it will catch me!"
As Swallow shot away, he saw someone familiar below. The girl who was selling eggs now stood outside a building. She was with other children.
Swallow perched in a tree to watch.
The girl showed the jewel to the others. "We'll never go hungry again!"
The children cheered.
Swallow's heart swelled. "I must tell Prince about this before leaving!"
But when Swallow reached the statue, he saw a crowd. Some people looked sad, others angry.
"Our beautiful statue is ruined!" a woman cried. "Two of its jewels are gone!"
"We must find the thief!" a man shouted. "Our Happy Prince is turning ugly."
"Ugly?" Swallow scowled. "That's not nice! And his beauty shines—in all his generous deeds. You people should thank him!"
Only the statue heard Swallow's words. "It's okay, Swallow. I don't need thanks. It's the right thing to do. Tell me, why have you returned?"
"I came to tell you how happy the orphans are," Swallow said.
"That's wonderful," said the statue. "My heart feels a bit lighter now. But you'd better leave for Egypt. A storm is coming."
Swallow looked up. The sky was gray, and it started to rain.
"I was planning to fly to Egypt with a ship. But it won't sail in this weather. I'll stay one more night."
He curled up in the warm spot between the statue's feet. But he couldn't sleep. He had an idea.
Later, after the storm, Swallow flew to the statue's shoulder. "You have one jewel left. Before I go, let me take it to someone in need."
"Yes," said the statue. "Take it to the three children who live under the bridge."
Swallow plucked the sapphire and flew toward the bridge. He passed many people who needed help.
"I wish I could help everyone," he thought.
Swallow found the three children huddled under the bridge. They were thin and cold, with no blankets or coats.
Swoosh! He dropped the jewel in their pot. As he flew off, he heard them shout.
"Was that a bird?" the boy cried.
"Yes, and it gave us a jewel!" his sister said. "Now we can buy clothing!"
"And food!" the littlest one shouted.
